AGENTS.md — readmit Development Guidelines

Source: AGENTS.md

Project context

readmit is an R package implementing the Readmission Risk Pool (RRP) analytical platform. The package is intended for distribution through CRAN and should follow conventional R package development practices.

This repository is being developed with an emphasis on delivering useful analytical functionality through a simple, understandable, and maintainable implementation.

1. Structure Before Sophistication

Structure Before Sophistication is the guiding development philosophy.

Establish the overall structure and end-to-end workflows before deeply implementing individual components.

Favor minimal working implementations that demonstrate the intended functionality. Expand and refine those implementations incrementally as requirements become clearer, users encounter issues, and practical needs emerge.

Do not introduce sophistication simply to anticipate every possible future requirement.

2. Prefer conventional R package practices

Use established R package conventions and tooling wherever possible.

  • Treat CRAN as an intended distribution channel.
  • Use R CMD check as the primary mechanism for validating package structure and compliance.
  • Use conventional R documentation, dependency management, and testing practices.
  • Prefer established R ecosystem solutions over custom infrastructure.

Do not create parallel systems for concerns already adequately addressed by standard R package tooling.

3. Implement only necessary complexity

Focus development effort on the functionality required to make RRP work as intended.

  • Prefer straightforward implementations over elaborate abstractions.
  • Build the minimum functionality necessary to support the current objective.
  • Write focused tests that establish the correctness of meaningful behavior.
  • Address real defects and demonstrated requirements rather than attempting to anticipate every possible edge case.
  • Avoid enterprise-style software qualification, excessive defensive programming, and elaborate validation or lifecycle machinery unless specifically warranted.

Complexity is acceptable when it materially supports core functionality, analytical correctness, or the user experience. It should not be introduced merely as a precaution or engineering exercise.

4. Prioritize human maintainability

The package should remain understandable and maintainable by its human maintainer.

Use clear organization, readable code, familiar R idioms, and appropriately scoped functions.

Some complexity is inevitable, and understanding sophisticated analytical functionality may require studying its implementation. However, avoid unnecessary layers of indirection, fragmented abstractions, or intricate dependencies that make the codebase difficult to navigate.

When choosing between implementations, favor the simpler approach that adequately satisfies the current requirements.

5. Develop iteratively and pragmatically

Favor a practical development cycle:

Establish structure → Implement minimal functionality → Test → Use → Refine

Ship coherent, working functionality rather than delaying progress to achieve exhaustive theoretical completeness.

Use conventional package checks and targeted tests to establish reasonable confidence. Introduce additional safeguards when actual behavior, defects, or requirements justify them.

Maintain essential correctness, particularly for analytical results and persistent user data, without expanding validation into a separate engineering objective.

Guiding principle

Build a rigorous analytical product, not an elaborate software system surrounding it.

Every additional abstraction, dependency, validation mechanism, or operational process should have a clear purpose tied to RRP’s functionality, correctness, usability, or maintainability.

R Package Development Conventions

  • Follow established R package conventions. Use R Packages (2e) by Hadley Wickham and Jenny Bryan as a preferred reference for package structure, development workflows, documentation, testing, dependency management, and general best practices. Treat its guidance as a strong convention rather than a strict rule; favor practical decisions appropriate to this package.

  • Prefer minimal, purposeful dependencies. Keep external dependencies to those that provide meaningful value. Prefer base R for straightforward operations when it offers a reasonably simple, readable solution rather than introducing a dependency for convenience alone. Use established packages when they materially improve clarity, functionality, maintainability, or development efficiency. Avoid unnecessary dependency avoidance that would result in more complex custom code.
